paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I had a guy sit next to me on the airplane. When the flight attendant came up to me, she was like, oh, thank you for being 1K with United, which is their highest status. Almost. It's like the highest level of VIP. Almost the highest level of VIP. They have a super secret level. I got in it for one year. And then I got booted out. But if you're listening, United, I would love to join again. I'm loyal to you, I'm not going anywhere.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So the guy turned to me and he said, well, how much do you have to fly to get that status? And I was trying to value what this guy actually needed. What was he actually asking me? Because it turns out he flies all the time. But there's not many direct flights out of Guadalajara to the United States, so you have to do all these weird things to get places. And I realized for him it had to do with money, because I sensed it. So I said, oh yeah, you have to spend — I'm not telling you guys how much we spend, it's not my money that gets spent on flights, but it's a lot of money. When I said the number, I was like, it's ridiculous how much money that is.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And then this guy — I'm trying to prepare for today's class, because all the ideas were going through my mind while I was flying. And I'm watching this guy, he's drinking espresso martinis at 10 in the morning. No uno, no dos, no tres, no cuatro — cinco martinis.

paragraphs.speaker: Interpreter
paragraphs.text: Not one, not two, not three, not four — five martinis.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: With espresso. I was like, this guy's gonna break. And he did. He did not get any social cues from me that I did not want to talk to him. He wasn't able to read my body language. And he kept talking to me, because he was caffeinated and he was drunk. I remember how that felt at 3 a.m. back in my twenties.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So I'm sitting there and I'm like, okay, why do I have to see this? What karma did I plant to see this? But as I was listening to him, almost every other comment was about how expensive everything is. He kept telling me how much the houses cost in Zapopan, how much the houses cost in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. And then how much the plane cost before COVID and how much it cost after COVID. He was like un abuelito, pues, «Cuando yo tenía 10 años, costaba 5 dólares; pero ahora cuesta 5000...» It’s exactly how we was like.

paragraphs.speaker: Interpreter
paragraphs.text: He was like a grandpa saying, oh, when I was 15 years old, I could buy tons of these; now I could only one…

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: That’s was a good translation. But I realized, in this guy's mind, he had these beliefs about money. Everything in this person's world was about: things cost too much. And then the corollary was that he didn't have enough. Like, if you want to see what bothers someone the most, give them caffeine and alcohol, and then they won't shut up about their problems. It was painful to listen — not only because I wanted to do something else, but more importantly, I was like, this is this person's reality, in his subconscious mind, all the time.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So there are certain scripts running in his mind that are just automatic. What's the word in Spanish for script?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Guiones.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Guiones. And that one's a little bit obvious. But in our own minds, there are so many things that just happen automatically. And those scripts are determining your reality, and you don't even know what's happening. And most of us have no idea that it's happening, that it'll shape our life, until it's too late.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So my question is: how can we first develop a kind of awareness that can see them without activating them? I mean, how many people here have had a goal, or an idea, or a dream that they wanted, but it just never materialized?
{audience raising hands}

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Yes. Me too. And then the question I've always had is: well, why didn't I do that? Why did I make that choice then that somehow makes me believe that I can't do it anymore? Like, what stopped me at the time? Why didn't I take those additional steps? Or why did I pause? Or why did I go right instead of left? So that's what we're going to investigate today and tomorrow.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: By the way, this person's a new translator right here. {pointing to someone} I don't know her, but I know she knows English very well. She’s hearing it. I'm just planting seeds. What was your name again?

paragraphs.speaker: Interpreter
paragraphs.text: Miriam.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Thank you. And for all of you who are teachers, just so you know, this is also a moment of teacher training right now. That was not what I planned to say for the first hour. So I'm now reconfiguring the whole class. The plan that I have is different now. And part of that has to do with you, because you're here. And this is not me talking at you — we're co-creating something. So it seems like I'm up here talking and sharing some things about myself, but there's a co-creation happening. Like, what's needed in the room?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And I'm sorry for those online, I can't see your faces. But turn on your cameras so everyone else online can see you, please. I can see it happening. Thank you. Because I have this goal in life that in any class that I teach, everyone actually turns on the camera — and it never happens.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I've tried. I tried being gruñón (grumpy). I tried being very sweet. I've tried offering money. I've tried the seed route — like, it's good seeds to turn on the camera. When you're in person, you can't hide your face. So why are you hiding behind the camera?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And so I'm going to ask a question for all of you online: why hide your face? Like, what are you thinking? What are you feeling in that moment? And these are the kind of questions we're going to ask ourselves over the next two days.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I used to absolutely — I hate watching myself on camera. I used to hide myself on the camera. I hated listening to my voice. Literally, my organs would shrivel up really, really small in my body when I would have to listen to myself. And then I was like, why? I had a confidence on stage. So I thought. But when I had to watch myself on a recording, I realized that that feeling was actually present when I was on stage. And then I was doing all of these things to be the opposite. In English, we call it posturing. It's when someone is overconfident, and it's not real confidence — you're pretending, and everyone knows you're just compensating for something. And so I thought I was confident, but I was compensating for this really tiny feeling I had inside.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: This is getting personal. I didn't expect this. This feeling that I wasn't worthwhile, that I didn't have anything to offer, that people don't like me. That I was unattractive and no one wanted to look at me. Like, I couldn't even look at myself.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And about maybe six months ago, somebody sent me a picture from Casa Salesiana. We had a retreat there — one of the first retreats we had. And it was a picture of me just sitting there watching the teachings. It was Gina. I looked at that photo, and I was like — I'm going to swear right now, I'm sorry — I was like, what the fuck. I looked at that for a minute. I looked at myself and I was like, God damn, you were hot. I was strong.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But that person who was in that picture at that time did not feel that at all. That person felt completely unattractive, small, worthless, and had nothing to offer to anyone. This is why I need my compadres. My buddies. Gina sent me this photo and she was like, you remember who you used to be, Tim?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And again, I asked myself this question. The reaction I had was — I grieved for that person. There was a deep pain that I had for that person 15 years ago. And then I was like, oh my God, how much of my life did I waste believing that? I was 32 years old in that picture. And the years just keep adding on, as we know. I'm never going to look that young again in this life. It's not about the external — it's about the internal. That view: what did that view create for me?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So I've been asking myself the question, like, what changed?
{Gina is showing the picture} Thanks, Gina. It’s fine. Now I can watch myself on camera too. I can listen to my voice.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: When I first started teaching — I'm just sitting in my room on Zoom teaching during COVID — I recognized I had this habit, and that habit was I would always touch my face. I did a lot like this. And somebody pointed it out to me. And the way that I felt in that moment was — the whole inside again collapsed. There was a collapse of my innards. And that's when I knew, okay, we had to change something. Because I can't sit on Zoom and get a bunch of pimples every day touching my face. And it's distracting, obviously, for the people watching too. It was a nervous habit. But it wasn't just a habit. It was reflecting a view of self. And so I was like, I need to go on this journey to figure out how to change that.
